description: Estudiantes de 4to y 5to año del Instituto Aonikenk con orientación en Ciencias Naturales. Nuestro enfoque integra biología, astronomía, diseño gráfico y programación para el desarrollo de proyectos interdisciplinarios.
summary: MARS NAVIGATOR is a web prototype of a surface-navigation and assistance tool for those future astronauts who will explore Mars. It will be demonstrated in a simulated crewed mission at Jezero Crater.
details:
MARS NAVIGATOR is a bilingual (English/Spanish) web prototype of a surface-navigation and assistance tool for those future astronauts who will explore Mars. This web will be demonstrated in a simulated crewed mission at Jezero Crater.

Moving safely across Mars means knowing how steep the ground is, how dangerously cold the wheather is, and where scientific targets such as water-related minerals or ice may lie, often with gloves on and no time to read dense screens.

The app combines an interactive map of Mars with security, temperature and mineral layers, a route planner that compares three alternative paths across a local sector and a voice-enabled assistant (ARIA). It runs entirely in browsers using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Canvas 2D. The current version uses simulated data, based on or inspired by publicly available information from official sources but not extracted from them. Apart from that, every value carries a data-quality label, and the system never declares a route safe without sufficient data. Moreover, It lies on showing how mapping, science data and voice interaction.

What exactly does it do?

MARS NAVIGATOR is a navigation and mission-support prototype that helps future Mars explorers understand the ground, its risks and routes before and during a surface traverse. It allows users to:

• Explore a global map of Mars, showing the whole area and demostrating the different places, their temperature, mineral layers, the slope overlay and 13 sites of interests, such as Jezero, Gale, Olympus Mons and Hellas.

• Inspect any place through a profile that separates Safety (temperature), Mobility (elevation and slope) and Scientific target (water-related minerals or ice), with expandable details and charts.

• Plan and compare three alternative routes (direct, balanced and the gentlest slope) for a rover or an EVA on foot, with distance, time, climb, slope, obstacles, difficulty and energy estimates.

• Preview the selected path in HOLO-VIEW, a simulated augmented-reality helmet visor with a first-person 3D view of the ground and an overlaid HUD.

• Interact by voice or text with ARIA, which is a rule-based assistant that searches places, describes the ground, calculates and compares routes, switches map layers and reads answers aloud.

• Track mission objectives, favorite places and an exploration logs for the simulated ARES-VII mission.

How does it work?

1. Simulated Data Layer: First, the app builds a global grid of 512 × 256 cells with elevation, slope, temperature and dominant-mineral values. Moreover, the grid is shaped after large, publicly known Martian features, such as Tharsis, Hellas, Valles Marineris and the north-south dichotomy. The 13 sites previously used are referencing the values simulated data. In a production version, these layers would be fed by MOLA / MOLA-HRSC elevation, THEMIS thermal data and CRISM/OMEGA mineral maps through Mars Trek and the PDS (future integration).

2. Map Visualization: The global map is drawn with Canvas 2D and supports zoom, search and layer switching. Also, a slope overlay highlights the steep regions. Each of these shows a data-quality label: REAL REFERENCE, HISTORICAL, ESTIMATED or SIMULATED.

3. Risk Assessment: Each place gets three prioritized alerts with an icon and a level word, so the meaning does not depend on color alone: CRITICAL, CAUTION, OK or TARGET. The labels (for example, night minimum below −100 °C, or slope above the vehicle's limit) were defined by the team for presentation only, and do not come from an official standard.

4. Local Sector Model: For route planning, the app generates a simulated 24 × 24 km sector at 150 m per pixel around the chosen site. It contains elevation, slope, boulder fields, sand areas, an estimated 14:00 local temperature and mineral patches. In a production version, this sector would use HiRISE digital ground models and images (future integration).

5. Route Planning: An A* search runs over the sector with three cost profiles and the vehicle's limits which are design assumptions: rover maximum 20° slope and 80 km range; EVA maximum 28° slope and 12 km range. The app computes metrics for each route and recommends one according to the user's priority (time, energy or gentlest terrain). Every route is marked "Safety: not verified", with a checklist to validate it before leaving.

6. HOLO-VIEW (mock-up): A ray-cast first-person 3D view of the simulated sector, with 2.5× vertical exaggeration, displays the route, compass, waypoints, position, ground warnings, environment values and simulated suit telemetry. It is activated from a drawn suit-sleeve button or an on-screen button. It is a visual simulation of an AR visor; it does not connect to real AR hardware.

7. ARIA Assistant: ARIA matches keywords in English or Spanish commands and runs the corresponding app action. Also, it uses the browser's Web Speech API for speech recognition (available, plus, speech synthesis to read answers aloud). All inputs and answers rely on the simulated data.

8. Mission Tools and Interface: Objectives, favorites places and logs are stored in the browser's local storage, and deletions can be undone. The interface uses progressive disclosure: one main task per screen, 1 to 3 status indicators at the top and secondary content in expandable sections. It also offers touch targets of at least 48 px, dark mode by default, a high-contrast mode, keyboard focus outlines and an English/Spanish switch.

What benefits does it have?

• Safety: It separates critical information (cold, steep slopes, terrain hazards) from general information, and never presents a route as safe without sufficient data.

• Efficiency: It shows the next action within each screen, and compares route alternatives side by side, reducing decision time for a busy explorer.

• Scientific: It puts water-related minerals and ice on the foreground as science targets, and clearly labels where each value comes from.

• Educational: It lets students and the public explore real Martian places, landforms and missions history in an interactive, bilingual format.

• Accessibility: Large controls are suited to gloved use, high-contrast mode, labels for screen readers and two languages.

What do you hope to achieve?

In short term, this app will replace the simulated layers with real data: Mars Trek map tiles, MOLA / MOLA-HRSC elevation, HiRISE terrain models for local sectors, THEMIS thermal data and CRISM mineral maps. Besides, it will add a radiation layer based on MSL RAD and MAVEN measurements. This layer does not exist in the current prototype.

In long term, this app will grow the prototype into a decision-support tool that mission planners and crews could test in analog missions, and scale to any Martian site where high-resolution ground data exists. It could also serve as an open educational resource about Mars exploration.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

• Development Tools: Claude (Anthropic) for code generation; Node.js for syntax checks; Python with Playwright and headless Google Chrome for automated visual and functional testing.

• Infrastructure and Hosting: Published as a web page on claude.ai (Claude artifact); no backend or database.

• Frontend & UI: Plain HTML and CSS; Canvas 2D for maps, charts, the 3D globe and HOLO-VIEW; inline SVG for icons and the suit sleeve; Google Fonts (Rajdhani, Inter, JetBrains Mono).

• Programming Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the app; Python for the test scripts.

• AI & Machine Learning: Claude Opus 5.5 for development; the browser's Web Speech API for speech recognition and synthesis. No machine-learning model is integrated into the app.

• Data Processing: In-browser procedural generation (value noise, fractal noise and feature models), A* pathfinding, and slope and shading computations.

• Software & Design: Cap Cut and Canva to create the creative video.

• Hardware: Computers with Windows 11 and macOS Tahoe 26.6.2. Also we used Spartphones with android and IOs

• Data Sources: Simulated data created for this prototype, based on publicly available information from official sources (not extracted from them).

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

• Claude (Anthropic, Claude Opus 5.5): Generated the full application code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and designed the interface, the HOLO-VIEW simulation and the bilingual redesign. Additionally, tt created the procedural ground, temperature and mineral models and the A* route planner, wrote the interface texts and English/Spanish translations, ran automated tests and drafted this project description.

The approximate reference values for the sites previously mentioned, come from Claude's general knowledge of published information and are labeled accordingly.

• Browser speech recognition (Web Speech API; in Chrome, a Google service): Converts spoken commands into text for the ARIA assistant. Availability depends on the browser.

• Browser and operating-system speech synthesis: Reads place profiles, route comparisons and assistant answers aloud.

• In-app assistant (ARIA): ARIA is not a machine-learning model. In fact, it analyzes the text of a command (typed or recognized from speech) by matching keywords in English or Spanish. Then, it runs an app action: searching a site, describing the ground, calculating, comparing or timing routes, showing steep areas, switching layers, logging points or controlling HOLO-VIEW. It returns a text and spoken answer, and all data it reports are simulated.

• AI-generated content was reviewed by the team.

NASA Data

The current prototype uses simulated data, based on or inspired by official NASA resources but not extracted from them. The following NASA resources were used as references and are the intended sources for a production version.

• JPL Mars Trek – https://trek.nasa.gov/mars/ – future integration (base map tiles, elevation and thematic layers).

• USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping Program, interactive maps of Mars – https://astrogeology-usgs.hub.arcgis.com/pages/interactive-maps-mars – future integration (geologic context for sites and sectors).

• Mars Perseverance Raw Images Gallery – https://mars.nasa.gov/mars2020/multimedia/raw-images/ – future integration (real imagery for the Jezero Crater site profile).

• Curiosity's proposed path up Mount Sharp – https://science.nasa.gov/resource/curiositys-proposed-path-up-mount-sharp/ – future integration (a real traverse to compare against the route planner at Gale Crater).

• Published Mars elevation and mission information (MOLA-based elevations of named sites; landing sites and findings of Perseverance, Curiosity, Opportunity, Viking 2 and Zhurong) – used as reference for the simulation. These figures were entered manually as approximate values; no files were downloaded.

Datasets that would feed each simulated layer in a production version:

• Ground elevation and slope (global map): MOLA / MOLA-HRSC blended elevation model, via Mars Trek or the PDS Geosciences Node (https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/) – future integration.

• Local sector terrain, boulders and sand (route planning): HiRISE imagery and digital terrain models (https://www.uahirise.org/) – future integration.

• Surface temperature: THEMIS (https://themis.asu.edu/) – future integration.

• Mineralogy and water-related minerals: CRISM products archived in the PDS (https://pds.nasa.gov/) – future integration.

• Subsurface ice: SHARAD radar results – future integration.

• Radiation (layer not yet implemented): MSL RAD and MAVEN SEP measurements – future integration.

• Points of interest and routes: The mission points (delta front, margin carbonates, crater C-12, dune field) and all routes are fictional and simulated. In production, they would be defined from HiRISE and Mars Trek data – future integration.

Space Agency Partner & Other Data

• USGS Astrogeology Science Center – https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/ – future integration (cartographic products and planetary nomenclature).

• ESA Mars Express HRSC (part of the MOLA-HRSC blended elevation model) – future integration.

• ESA Mars Express OMEGA (mineral mapping) – future integration.

• Mars Climate Database (LMD / ESA-supported) – http://www-mars.lmd.jussieu.fr/ – future integration (surface temperature and pressure modeling).

Simulated dataset created for this prototype:

• How it was created: it was generated in the browser with JavaScript using seeded random numbers and noise functions, then shaped by simple models of known large features (Tharsis volcanoes, Hellas, Argyre and Isidis basins, Valles Marineris, the north-south dichotomy, the north polar cap).

• Variables: Global grid with elevation, slope, maximum daytime temperature and dominant-mineral class. Local 24 × 24 km sector with elevation, slope, terrain hazard (boulders or sand), estimated 14:00 temperature and mineral class. Simulated suit telemetry, wind, Sol 412 and the ARES-VII mission scenario.

• Area: The whole planet at about 0.7° per cell, plus local sectors around each named site, with Jezero Crater as the mission base.

• What it is based on: Publicly known topography, approximate published elevations of named sites, general mineral distributions reported by orbital missions, and general Martian temperature ranges. It was not extracted from any of these sources, and all values are illustrative.

• Images and graphics: The app uses no external images. All maps, the globe, charts, the HOLO-VIEW ground and the suit sleeve are generated by the app's own code (Canvas 2D and inline SVG). Fonts come from Google Fonts (Rajdhani, Inter, JetBrains Mono), distributed under the SIL Open Font License. Some icons are emoji characters rendered by the user's operating system.
